subject: ela
intro: Comparing a written text to an audio, video, or live version means noticing what each one can do that the other cannot. Print lets you imagine and gives you a character's exact words and thoughts. Audio, film, and live performance add real sound, music, voices, faces, and movement. For each item, read the written lines and the short description of the other version, then name one clear thing the version adds or shows that the words alone do not.

items.prompt: Read the line: 'Nate said he was not scared, and he kept his eyes on the door.' In a film version, the actor playing Nate speaks the line in a shaky voice and his hands tremble. Name one thing the film shows that the written line alone does not.
items.answer: The film shows that Nate is actually scared, through his shaky voice and trembling hands.

steps: The written line only reports Nate's words ('he was not scared') and that he watched the door.
The film adds a shaky voice and trembling hands, which are sights and sounds the words do not give.
These added details reveal that Nate is frightened even though he claims he is not, something the print left for the reader to guess.

items.prompt: Read the excerpt: 'The hallway was empty. A single light flickered at the far end.' In an audio recording of this story, slow creaking sounds and a low hum play under the narrator's voice during these lines. What does the audio version add that the written text does not include?
items.answer: The audio adds real sound effects, the creaking and the low hum, which the written text cannot provide.

steps: The written text describes only an empty hallway and a flickering light.
The audio version adds creaking sounds and a low hum, which are actual sounds the print cannot make.
These sounds make the hallway feel eerie, while the text describes the scene in silent words only.

items.prompt: Read the poem lines: 'Tap, tap, tap went the rain, / soft on the windowpane.' In an audio version, a reader speaks the lines gently and a real tapping sound plays behind the words. Name one thing hearing this version gives you that reading the lines silently does not.
items.answer: Hearing it gives you the real tapping sound and the gentle voice, so you actually hear the rhythm of the rain instead of only picturing it.

steps: Reading silently, you see the repeated word 'tap' and imagine the rain in your own mind.
The audio adds an actual tapping sound and a gentle speaking voice, which print cannot make.
So the listener hears the rhythm and softness of the rain, a sound experience the written page leaves to the imagination.

items.prompt: Read the description: 'The robot was taller than a grown man and made of shining metal.' In a movie version, the robot is shown as a blue machine with glowing red eyes and heavy stomping feet. Name one thing the movie shows that the written description does not.
items.answer: The movie shows the robot's exact look and motion, such as its blue color, glowing red eyes, and stomping feet, which the words do not state.

steps: The written description gives only the robot's height and that it is shining metal.
The movie fixes an exact image: a blue color, glowing red eyes, and the sound of stomping feet.
These specific details are added by the film; the text left the robot's color, eyes, and sound to each reader's imagination.

items.prompt: Read the stage direction and line from a drama: 'LILA (softly): It does not matter to me.' In a live performance, the actor playing Lila looks down at the floor and her voice breaks as she says the line. Name one thing the live performance shows that the script's words alone do not.
items.answer: The performance shows that it does matter to Lila, through her looking down and her breaking voice.

steps: The script tells us only that Lila speaks softly and says it does not matter to her.
The live actor adds a downward look and a breaking voice, which an audience can see and hear.
These choices reveal that Lila is hurt and that it really does matter, a feeling the words alone hide.

items.prompt: Read the line: 'Come in,' said the old woman, and she smiled. In a film version, the actor playing the old woman smiles but narrows her eyes in a sly way as she speaks. What does the film add that the written line does not?
items.answer: The film adds a sly, narrowed-eye look that makes the smile seem untrustworthy, which the written line does not show.

steps: The written line says only that the woman invites the guest in and smiles.
The film actor adds narrowed, sly eyes, a facial expression the words do not describe.
This look suggests the woman may not be friendly, changing how the moment feels, while the text shows a plain smile.

items.prompt: Read the excerpt: 'The crowd cheered as the runner crossed the line first.' In a video version, you see thousands of fans waving flags and hear a roar of voices filling the stadium. Name one thing the video shows or lets you hear that the written sentence does not.
items.answer: The video lets you see the waving flags and hear the real roar of the crowd, sights and sounds the sentence only names.

steps: The written sentence reports that the crowd cheered and the runner won.
The video adds the visible flags and the actual roaring sound of thousands of voices.
These real images and sounds make the moment feel huge, while the text simply tells you the crowd cheered.

items.prompt: Read the poem lines: 'The drum began to pound, / boom, boom, across the town.' In an audio version, a deep drumbeat plays loudly under the words as the reader speaks. What does the audio version give the listener that the printed poem does not?
items.answer: The audio gives the listener the actual deep drumbeat sound, which the printed poem can only describe in words.

steps: On the page, the words 'boom, boom' describe the drum, and the reader imagines the sound.
The audio adds a real, loud drumbeat that the listener actually hears.
Hearing the pounding drum makes the rhythm physical, something print can name but cannot produce.

items.prompt: Read the line: 'I'm fine,' Marcus muttered, and he turned back to his book. In a film version, the actor playing Marcus says the line with a flat, tired voice and his shoulders slump. Name one thing the film shows about Marcus that the written line alone does not.
items.answer: The film shows that Marcus is sad or worn down, through his flat, tired voice and slumped shoulders.

steps: The written line tells us only that Marcus says he is fine and goes back to his book.
The film adds a flat, tired tone of voice and slumped shoulders, which an audience can hear and see.
These added details suggest Marcus is not really fine, a feeling the print leaves unstated.

items.prompt: Read the description: 'A forest stretched out below them, green and endless.' In a movie version, the camera flies high over a wide green forest while soft music plays. Name one thing the movie adds that the written description does not include.
items.answer: The movie adds the soft background music, a sound the written description cannot provide.

steps: The written description tells us the forest is green and looks endless.
The movie adds soft music playing over the wide view, which is a sound print cannot make.
The music gives the scene a peaceful feeling that the words alone do not supply.

items.prompt: Read the stage direction and line: 'GREG (loudly): Get out of my way!' In a live performance, the actor playing Greg steps forward and points his finger at the other character before he shouts. What does the live performance show that the script's words do not?
items.answer: The performance shows Greg's threatening movement, stepping forward and pointing, which the script's words do not describe.

steps: The script tells us only that Greg shouts the line loudly.
The live actor adds a step forward and a pointing finger, actions the audience can see.
These movements make Greg seem more aggressive, adding to the words a physical threat the script alone does not show.

items.prompt: Read the excerpt: 'Snow fell quietly over the sleeping village.' In an audio recording, soft, slow piano music plays while the narrator reads the line in a calm voice. Name one thing the audio version adds that the written sentence does not.
items.answer: The audio adds the soft piano music and a calm speaking voice, sounds the written sentence cannot provide.

steps: The written sentence describes snow falling quietly over a sleeping village.
The audio adds slow piano music and a calm narrator's voice, which are real sounds print cannot make.
These sounds make the scene feel peaceful and sleepy, while the text describes the snow in silent words.

items.prompt: Read the line: 'The dog growled at the stranger.' In a video version, you hear a deep, low growl and see the dog's fur stand up and its teeth show. Name one thing the video lets you see or hear that the written line does not.
items.answer: The video lets you hear the real growl and see the dog's raised fur and bared teeth, details the written line only names in part.

steps: The written line tells us only that the dog growled at the stranger.
The video adds the actual sound of the growl and the sight of raised fur and showing teeth.
These real sights and sounds make the dog seem clearly dangerous, while the text simply states that it growled.

items.prompt: Read the description: 'The queen wore a long gown for the ball.' In a film version, the queen's gown is shown as deep purple with gold trim and a sparkling crown sits on her head. What does the film show that the written description does not?
items.answer: The film shows the gown's exact colors and the crown, such as the deep purple, gold trim, and sparkle, which the words do not state.

steps: The written description says only that the queen wore a long gown.
The film fixes an exact image: deep purple with gold trim and a sparkling crown.
These specific details are added by the film; the text left the gown's color and the crown to the reader's imagination.

items.prompt: Read the poem lines: 'The wind howled through the trees, / wild and cold all night.' In an audio version, a real whooshing wind sound plays under the reader's voice. Name one thing the audio version gives the listener that reading the lines silently does not.
items.answer: The audio gives the listener the real whooshing wind sound, which reading silently can only imagine.

steps: Reading silently, you see the word 'howled' and picture the wind in your own mind.
The audio adds an actual whooshing wind sound that the listener hears.
Hearing the wind makes it feel real and present, a sound the printed page can describe but cannot produce.
